note: Hand-curated Mumbai Metropolitan Region water facts (v2, regionalised). Ordered as a narrative: the region's structure and supply first, then equity, groundwater, rivers, floods, and the coast. Greater Mumbai (BMC) facts are flagged as such where the figure is city-specific; regional figures span the nine MMR corporations. Figures from BMC, Praja Foundation, MMRDA, CPCB/MPCB, the India Water Portal (Tiwale), Question of Cities, NGT orders, IITM and contemporary press; see each fact's source. facts.title: Nine cities, one contested source pool
facts.interpretation: The Mumbai Metropolitan Region is served by nine municipal corporations - Greater Mumbai (BMC), Thane, Navi Mumbai, Kalyan-Dombivli, Mira-Bhayandar, Vasai-Virar, Bhiwandi-Nizampur, Ulhasnagar and Panvel - drawing on a shared, contested set of dams. There is no single regional water utility, so a surplus in one city and rationing in the next are negotiated between separate bodies over the same rivers.
facts.source_label: India Water Portal (Sachin Tiwale, ATREE); MMRDA

facts.title: Mumbai takes two-thirds of the region's water
facts.interpretation: Greater Mumbai commands about 67% of the MMR's developed water resources. In 1999 the Pinjal source, originally earmarked for Vasai-Virar, was reallocated to Mumbai - an early sign of how the core city's claims override the periphery's. The further a corporation sits from Mumbai, the less water its residents get.

facts.title: Greater Mumbai's supply gap
facts.interpretation: Praja Foundation's 2024 audit puts BMC supply at about 3,975 million litres a day against a demand of 4,664 - a ~15% (689 MLD) shortfall, rationed unevenly across the city before a single litre is lost to leaks. And this is the best-supplied corporation in the region.
facts.source_label: Praja Foundation - Status of Civic Issues in Mumbai 2024

facts.title: Non-revenue water (leaks + theft)
facts.interpretation: The BMC's own 2024 audit puts non-revenue water at about 34% - roughly 1,343 MLD lost to leaks, metering gaps and theft every day, up from 27% in 2018. That lost volume alone is close to Greater Mumbai's entire supply-demand gap.

facts.title: Half of Bengaluru's connections, twice its people
facts.interpretation: Greater Mumbai has just 5.5 lakh water connections for over 1.2 crore people - roughly 23 people per connection - because BMC counts connections per building: one connection typically serves an entire society, chawl or slum cluster. Bengaluru's plotted low-rise pattern yields nearly twice as many connections for a smaller population. Connection counts are not comparable across cities, and none of them says how many households a pipe actually reaches.
facts.source_label: Praja Foundation, Status of Civic Issues in Mumbai (May 2025), RTI Table 5 - as on March 2025

facts.title: Greater Mumbai's seven lakes
facts.interpretation: BMC is supplied entirely by seven impounded lakes - Bhatsa, Upper Vaitarna, Middle Vaitarna, Modak Sagar, Tansa, Vihar and Tulsi. Bhatsa alone provides about 48% of the city's water; Vihar and Tulsi, the two oldest (1860 and 1879), under 3% between them. The other corporations draw on their own dams - Barvi for the eastern corridor, the Surya scheme for the west, Morbe for Navi Mumbai.

facts.title: The scramble for new sources
facts.interpretation: The region is chasing new supply on every side. The Surya scheme (403 MLD) began feeding Vasai-Virar in November 2023, with Mira-Bhayandar's 218 MLD phase still in build; the Kalu dam (1,140 MLD), long stalled by forest and tribal-displacement disputes, is meant for Thane, Bhiwandi, Kalyan-Dombivli and Ulhasnagar. Each is run by a different agency - MMRDA, KIDC, the corporations - with no single plan.

facts.title: BMC's eighth source: Gargai dam
facts.interpretation: In December 2025 the BMC floated a Rs 3,000 crore tender for the Gargai dam in Palghar, Mumbai's first new water source since Middle Vaitarna in 2014. It would add about 440 MLD but submerge roughly 2,100 acres of the Tansa Wildlife Sanctuary forest and displace some 619 tribal families.
facts.source_label: BMC tender (Dec 2025); Land Conflict Watch project record (619 families, ~2,100 acres of Tansa sanctuary forest submerged)

facts.title: A 3.6x water gap across one metro
facts.interpretation: Per-capita supply inside the same region ranges from about 252 litres a day in Mumbai to 105 in Mira-Bhayandar, 100 in Bhiwandi and just 70 in Vasai-Virar - against a CPHEEO norm of 135-150. The gap between the core city and its neighbours rivals the gap between rich and poor inside Mumbai itself.

facts.title: Slum vs non-slum access, within Mumbai
facts.interpretation: Praja Foundation's 2024 audit finds metered slum households in Greater Mumbai receive about 45 litres per person per day against 135 for non-slum households - a threefold gap inside the wealthiest corporation (the CPHEEO service norm itself is 135-150 LPCD). A peer-reviewed study (Mandala et al. 2023) finds non-notified slums use 38% less than notified ones even after controlling for income and religion.
facts.source_label: Praja Foundation - Status of Civic Issues in Mumbai 2024

facts.title: Wards with 24x7 supply
facts.interpretation: Only one of Greater Mumbai's 24 administrative wards (T / Mulund) receives round-the-clock water. Citywide the average supply is about 5.37 hours a day, and roughly 71% of zones get under four hours - the inequality is in duration and pressure, not only in volume.

facts.title: What a slum household pays for water
facts.interpretation: Households that fall outside the piped network buy from tankers at roughly Rs 729 per person a month, against about Rs 25 for a metered connection - the poorest pay the most. An April 2025 tanker strike pushed the BMC to invoke the Disaster Management Act, the first known use of it for a water-distribution dispute.

facts.title: Excluded from the national groundwater assessment
facts.interpretation: Mumbai City and Mumbai Suburban are the only two of Maharashtra's 35 districts left out of the CGWB Dynamic Ground Water Resources Assessment - treated as fully urban and never measured as rural blocks. The platform now tracks 53 CGWB observation wells across the region (Mumbai plus Thane, Palghar and Raigad), but the 'safe / critical / over-exploited' stamp simply doesn't exist for the urban core, because no one measures it.
facts.source_label: India-WRIS / CGWB Ground Water Year Book of Maharashtra

facts.title: India's most polluted river stretch runs through Mumbai
facts.interpretation: In CPCB's October 2025 assessment the Mithi at Mahim records a maximum BOD of 210 mg/l - the worst of every polluted river stretch in India, against a 3 mg/l bathing criterion. The eastern corridor's Ulhas remains listed too, though in Priority V, the least severe class. Mumbai's other city rivers - Dahisar, Poisar, Oshiwara - do not appear in the national list at all: they are barely monitored as rivers, which is its own finding. Thane Creek, the region's shared sink, takes an estimated 1,260 MLD of sewage with BOD above the limit in every sample.
facts.source_label: CPCB, Polluted River Stretches for Restoration of Water Quality - 2025 (Oct 2025); Thane Creek WQ review 2025

facts.title: Raw sewage into Powai Lake
facts.interpretation: Powai Lake - home to the Indian marsh crocodile - takes about 18 million litres of untreated sewage a day (BMC's affidavit says ~10.9), and a treatment plant to stop it is not due until December 2027. Hyacinth cover is contested: BMC's April 2024 operational data says 23-25% of the surface, the July 2025 NGT-proceedings framing says 80%. An NGT-appointed committee has proposed a Rs 5 lakh-per-inlet monthly penalty on the BMC.
facts.source_label: NGT OA 150/2025 proceedings; BMC hyacinth-removal reporting (Mumbai Live, Apr 2024); Free Press Journal

facts.title: The 26 July 2005 deluge
facts.interpretation: On 26 July 2005 the Santacruz observatory recorded 944 mm of rain in a single day; the Maharashtra floods that followed killed more than a thousand people and remain the reference event for Mumbai's flood planning. The city floods when an intense cloudburst coincides with a high tide that shuts its gravity outfalls.

facts.title: A public flood model that stays private
facts.interpretation: iFLOWS-Mumbai, the city's integrated flood-warning system, was built with public money but briefs officials only - there is no public dashboard or API. The best openly available flood-precursor signal is the IITM Mumbai-rain mesh, India's only city-scale polarimetric-radar rainfall network, refreshing every 15 minutes.

facts.title: The climate budget's flood bill
facts.interpretation: Mumbai runs India's first city climate budget (from 2024), and Urban Flooding & Water Resource Management is its largest sector: Rs 15,048 crore allocated for FY 2025-26, up from Rs 9,708 crore budgeted in FY 2024-25 - of which Rs 7,439 crore was actually spent. Over the same two years the city's pre-monsoon flooding-spot list grew from 386 to 496. The budget report tracks flooding spots as one of its own performance indicators.
facts.source_label: BMC Climate Budget Report 2025-26 (Climate Action Cell, via OpenCity)

facts.title: Mangroves cleared for the Coastal Road
facts.interpretation: In March 2025 the Supreme Court allowed felling about 45,000 mangrove trees for the Coastal Road's northern extension. Mumbai has lost roughly 40% of its mangrove cover since 1991 - the same mangroves, with the city's salt pans, are its natural flood buffer.

facts.title: Salt-pan flood buffer handed for housing
facts.interpretation: The Union government approved transferring 256 acres of Mumbai's publicly-owned salt-pan land to the Adani-led Dharavi Redevelopment Project. Salt pans and mangroves together absorb tidal and monsoon surge; building over them is widely warned to deepen the city's flooding.

facts.title: Mahul: a resettlement colony ruled unfit to live in
facts.interpretation: The National Green Tribunal declared Mahul - a Chembur resettlement colony ringed by three refineries and 16 chemical plants - 'unfit for human habitation' in 2015. Many of its roughly 40,000 residents were evicted from along the Tansa drinking-water pipeline and then moved into the toxic zone. The order and the colony both stand as of 2026; the resident count has not been re-surveyed since.
